system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:ebb3ac98d950",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that observed empirical evidence discriminates between views of PSM exhaustiveness.",
  "did": "They explicitly stated the empirical observations give little evidence for weighing the views and used them only to make the perspectives concrete.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The observations are compatible with several perspectives, so they illustrate rather than settle the question."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:55190cc92095",
  "problem": "Whether to infer the prompt directly from the rubric verifier score or to decompose rubric elicitation into stages.",
  "did": "They adopted a two-stage approach (infer response y from rubric, then prompt x from y) after finding one-stage DPO performed significantly worse.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "one-stage DPO directly optimizing prompts based on the verifier score"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "One-stage DPO performed significantly worse than two-stage DPO in early experiments and in the in-distribution benchmark."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:e02cace13e9f",
  "problem": "How to evaluate the quality of natural-language feature descriptions of neurons without relying on costly human judgment.",
  "did": "They had an LM predict feature firing patterns from a description and checked whether the predictions matched real activations, then used this as a reward to train an explainer.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "previous more expensive approaches that relied on general-purpose chatbots"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "A description can be verified by simulating firing patterns and comparing to reality, giving a cheap scoring signal."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:d02e38070e0e",
  "problem": "How to design the task suite's difficulty distribution so that capability trends can be extrapolated.",
  "did": "They aim for a fairly uniform distribution of task difficulty spanning a wide range rather than a bimodal one.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "bimodal distribution of difficulty"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "A uniform distribution lets them meaningfully extrapolate gradual increases in task success instead of seeing rapid progress, stalls, then rapid progress again."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:1e4714620cbb",
  "problem": "Whether to withhold or publish a severe vulnerability in an old enrollment system that nobody could fix.",
  "did": "Sat on the Telebears vulnerability for four years rather than going public, because publishing would not reduce harm.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "go public immediately",
   "report to developers who could fix it"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Going public sooner wouldn't minimize harm: students couldn't stop using the system, no one was left to fix it, and the attack would be trivially exploitable once public."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:e69f777d91f9",
  "problem": "Whether to include the earlier TaskRabbit experiment in the report.",
  "did": "They excluded the TaskRabbit experiment from this report, pointing readers to a separate document.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It came from earlier iterations of the methodology and received more attention than anticipated."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:6dfd20cc08da",
  "problem": "Whether to keep adapting existing general-purpose coding agents or to build a task-specific agent.",
  "did": "After finding that direct prompting and prior agent frameworks failed, the authors dropped them and built an agent tailored to the benchmark.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "direct LLM prompting",
   "best-of-k sampling",
   "SWE-Bench-style agent frameworks"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prior frameworks were specialized to their own domains, and the errors encountered here differ in style from SWE-Bench errors, so they were poor at fixing them."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:9cd98cf3c6d7",
  "problem": "Whether negation-style annotations alone cause belief implantation, or whether stronger or different annotations can prevent it",
  "did": "Tested three interventions beyond simple prefix/suffix negations: repeated negations around every claim sentence, explicit corrections giving the true version, and local in-sentence negations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "more negations",
   "explicit corrections",
   "local negation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To find whether any form of negation prevents belief implantation."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:bd4aaeafc1b8",
  "problem": "What baseline to compare IP against to judge whether train-time prompt modification adds value beyond safety instructions at test time.",
  "did": "They used Pure Tuning, Safe Testing (PTST), inserting a safety instruction only at test time, as a baseline, adapting it to put the instruction in the user message.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "inserting the safety instruction in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "For consistency with their other experiments."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b176df93ea88",
  "problem": "Whether METR should expand into conducting third-party evaluations itself.",
  "did": "METR stated it is interested and may hire and fundraise, but made expansion conditional on external factors and open to other actors entering the space.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "other actors entering the space",
   "governments conducting audits in-house"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Expansion depends on whether governments mandate access, whether labs give access, hiring success, and whether it detracts from developing the science."
 }
]
